title: VI. The Prosecutor Catches Mitya
paragraphs: Something utterly unexpected and astonishing to Mitya followed. He could never, even a minute earlier, have imagined that anyone could treat him, Mitya Karamazov, like that. Worst of all, there was something humiliating about it, and on their side something “supercilious and scornful.” It was nothing to take off his coat, but he was asked to undress further — or rather, not asked, but “commanded,” and he understood that perfectly. Out of pride and contempt he submitted without a word. Several peasants accompanied the lawyers and stayed on the same side of the curtain. “To be ready if force is required,” Mitya thought, “and perhaps for some other reason, too.”

“Well, must I take off my shirt, too?” he asked sharply, but Nikolay Parfenovitch did not answer. He was busy with the prosecutor, examining the coat, the trousers, the waistcoat, and the cap; and it was clear that they were both very interested in what they were inspecting. “They make no bones about it,” Mitya thought, “they don’t bother with even the most basic courtesy.”
“I’m asking you for the second time — do I need to take off my shirt or not?” he said, still more sharply and irritably.
“Don’t worry yourself. We’ll tell you what to do,” Nikolay Parfenovitch said, and his voice was positively peremptory — or so it seemed to Mitya.

Meanwhile a consultation was going on in low voices between the lawyers. There turned out to be on the coat, especially on the left side at the back, a huge patch of blood, dry and still stiff. There were bloodstains on the trousers, too. What’s more, in the presence of the peasant witnesses, Nikolay Parfenovitch ran his fingers along the collar, the cuffs, and every seam of the coat and trousers, obviously looking for something — money, of course. He didn’t even hide from Mitya his suspicion that he might be capable of sewing money into his clothes.

“He treats me not like an officer but like a thief,” Mitya muttered to himself. They shared their thoughts with one another with astonishing frankness. The secretary, for instance, who was also behind the curtain, fussing about and listening, called Nikolay Parfenovitch’s attention to the cap, which they were also fingering.

“You remember Gridyenko, the copying-clerk,” the secretary observed. “Last summer he received the wages of the whole office, and pretended to have lost the money when he was drunk. And where was it found? Why, in just such pipings in his cap. The hundred-rouble notes were rolled up in little tubes and sewn into the piping.”
Both lawyers remembered Gridyenko’s case perfectly, and so they set Mitya’s cap aside and decided that all his clothes would have to be more thoroughly examined later.
“Excuse me,” cried Nikolay Parfenovitch suddenly, noticing that the right cuff of Mitya’s shirt was turned in and covered with blood, “excuse me, what’s that — blood?”
“Yes,” Mitya jerked out.
“That is — what blood?... And why is the cuff turned in?”
Mitya told him how he had gotten the sleeve stained with blood looking after Grigory, and had turned it inside when he was washing his hands at Perhotin’s.
“You must take off your shirt, too. That’s very important as material evidence.”
Mitya flushed red and flew into a rage.
“What, am I to stay naked?” he shouted.
“Don’t worry yourself. We’ll arrange something. And meanwhile, take off your socks.”
“You’re not joking? Is that really necessary?” Mitya’s eyes flashed.
“We are in no mood for joking,” Nikolay Parfenovitch answered sternly.

“Well, if I must —” muttered Mitya, and sitting down on the bed, he took off his socks. He felt unbearably awkward. All the others were clothed, while he was naked, and strange to say, when he was undressed he somehow felt guilty in their presence, and was almost ready to believe himself that he was inferior to them, and that they now had a perfect right to despise him.

“When everyone’s undressed, somehow there’s no shame in it, but when you’re the only one undressed and everyone’s looking, it’s degrading,” he kept saying to himself, over and over. “It’s like a dream, I’ve sometimes dreamed of being in such degrading positions.” It was agony for him to take off his socks. They were very dirty, and so was his underwear, and now everyone could see it. And what was worse, he disliked his own feet. All his life he had thought both his big toes hideous. He particularly loathed the coarse, flat, crooked nail on the right one, and now they would all see it. Feeling unbearably ashamed made him, at once and deliberately, rougher. He pulled off his shirt himself.
“Would you like to look anywhere else, if you aren’t ashamed to?”
“No, there’s no need to, at present.”
“Well, am I to stay naked like this?” he added savagely.
“Yes, that can’t be helped for the time being.... Kindly sit down here for a while. You can wrap yourself in a quilt from the bed, and I ... I’ll take care of all this.”

All the items were shown to the witnesses. The report of the search was drawn up, and at last Nikolay Parfenovitch went out, and the clothes were carried out after him. Ippolit Kirillovitch went out, too. Mitya was left alone with the peasants, who stood in silence, never taking their eyes off him. Mitya wrapped himself in the quilt. He felt cold. His bare feet stuck out, and he couldn’t pull the quilt over to cover them. Nikolay Parfenovitch seemed to be gone a long time, “an unbearable time.” “He thinks of me as a puppy,” Mitya thought, gnashing his teeth. “That rotten prosecutor has gone, too — out of contempt, no doubt; it disgusts him to see me naked!”

Mitya assumed, however, that his clothes would be examined and returned to him. But imagine his indignation when Nikolay Parfenovitch came back with completely different clothes, carried in behind him by a peasant.

“Here are some clothes for you,” he remarked airily, seeming quite pleased with the success of his errand. “Mr. Kalganov has kindly provided these for this unusual emergency, as well as a clean shirt. Luckily he had them all in his trunk. You can keep your own socks and underclothes.”
Mitya flew into a fury.
“I won’t have other people’s clothes!” he shouted menacingly. “Give me my own!”
“It’s impossible!”
“Give me my own. To hell with Kalganov and his clothes, too!”

It took a long time to persuade him. But somehow they managed to calm him down. They impressed upon him that his clothes, being stained with blood, had to be “included with the other material evidence,” and that they “had no right to let him have them now ... taking into consideration the possible outcome of the case.” Mitya at last understood this. He sank into gloomy silence and hurriedly dressed himself. He only remarked, as he put them on, that the clothes were much better than his old ones, and that he disliked “gaining by the change.” Besides, the coat was “ridiculously tight. Am I to be dressed up like a fool ... for your amusement?”

They urged him again that he was exaggerating, that Kalganov was only a little taller, so that only the trousers might be a bit too long. But the coat really did turn out to be tight in the shoulders.
“Damn it all! I can hardly button it,” Mitya grumbled. “Be so good as to tell Mr. Kalganov from me that I didn’t ask for his clothes, and it’s not my doing that they’ve dressed me up like a clown.”
“He understands that, and is sorry ... I mean, not sorry to lend you his clothes, but sorry about all this business,” mumbled Nikolay Parfenovitch.
“Damn his sorrow! Well, where now? Am I to go on sitting here?”

He was asked to go back to the “other room.” Mitya went in, scowling with anger, and trying to avoid looking at anyone. Dressed in another man’s clothes, he felt disgraced, even in the eyes of the peasants, and of Trifon Borissovitch, whose face appeared, for some reason, in the doorway, and vanished at once. “He’s come to look at me dressed up,” Mitya thought. He sat down on the same chair as before. He had an absurd, nightmarish feeling, as though he were out of his mind.

“Well, what now? Are you going to flog me? That’s all that’s left for you,” he said, clenching his teeth and addressing the prosecutor. He would not turn to Nikolay Parfenovitch, as though he disdained to speak to him.
“He looked too closely at my socks, and turned them inside out on purpose, to show everyone how dirty they were — the scoundrel!”
“Well, now we must proceed to the examination of witnesses,” Nikolay Parfenovitch observed, as though answering Mitya’s question.
“Yes,” said the prosecutor thoughtfully, as though reflecting on something.

“We’ve done what we could in your interest, Dmitri Fyodorovitch,” Nikolay Parfenovitch went on, “but having received from you such an uncompromising refusal to explain to us the source from which you obtained the money found upon you, we are, at the present moment —”
“What is the stone in your ring?” Mitya interrupted suddenly, as though coming out of a daze. He pointed to one of the three large rings on Nikolay Parfenovitch’s right hand.
“Ring?” repeated Nikolay Parfenovitch in surprise.
“Yes, that one ... on your middle finger, with the little veins in it — what stone is that?” Mitya persisted, like a peevish child.
“That’s a smoky topaz,” Nikolay Parfenovitch said, smiling. “Would you like to look at it? I’ll take it off ...”

“No, don’t take it off,” cried Mitya furiously, suddenly coming to himself and angry with himself. “Don’t take it off ... there’s no need.... Damn it!... Gentlemen, you’ve sullied my heart! Do you really suppose I would conceal it from you, if I had actually killed my father — that I would shuffle, lie, and hide myself? No, that’s not like Dmitri Karamazov, he couldn’t do that, and if I were guilty, I swear, I wouldn’t have waited for your arrival, or for sunrise as I first intended — I would have killed myself before this, without waiting for the dawn! I know that about myself now. I couldn’t have learned so much in twenty years as I’ve found out in this accursed night!... And would I be like this on this night, at this moment, sitting with you, could I have talked like this, could I have moved like this, could I have looked at you and at the world like this, if I had really been the murderer of my father — when the very thought of having accidentally killed Grigory gave me no peace all night? Not from fear — oh, not simply from fear of your punishment! From the disgrace of it! And you expect me to be open with scoffers like you, who see nothing and believe in nothing — blind moles and scoffers — and to tell you another filthy thing I’ve done, another disgrace, even if it would save me from your charge? No, better Siberia! The man who opened the door to my father and went in at that door, he killed him, he robbed him. Who was he? I’m racking my brain and can’t figure it out. But I can tell you it was not Dmitri Karamazov, and that’s all I can tell you, and that’s enough — enough, leave me alone.... Exile me, punish me, but don’t bother me any more. I’ll say no more. Call your witnesses!”

Mitya uttered his sudden monologue as though he had made up his mind to be completely silent from then on. The prosecutor watched him the entire time, and only when he had stopped speaking did he observe, as though it were the most ordinary thing, with the most frigid and composed air:

“Oh, about the open door you just spoke of, we may as well inform you, in passing, of a very interesting piece of evidence of the greatest importance both to you and to us, given to us by Grigory, the old man you wounded. Upon his recovery, in answer to our questions, he clearly and emphatically stated that when, on coming out to the steps and hearing a noise in the garden, he decided to enter it through the little gate that stood open, before he noticed you running — as you have already told us — in the dark from the open window where you had seen your father, he, Grigory, glanced to the left, and, while noticing the open window, also observed at the same time, much closer to him, the door, standing wide open — that very door which you have stated to have been shut the whole time you were in the garden. I will not conceal from you that Grigory himself confidently affirms and bears witness that you must have run out through that door, though of course he did not see you do so with his own eyes, since he only noticed you first some distance away in the garden, running toward the fence.”
Mitya had leapt up from his chair halfway through this speech.
“Nonsense!” he yelled in a sudden frenzy. “It’s a barefaced lie. He couldn’t have seen the door open, because it was shut. He’s lying!”
“I consider it my duty to repeat that he is firm in his statement. He does not waver. He sticks to it. We’ve cross-examined him several times.”
“Precisely. I have cross-examined him several times,” Nikolay Parfenovitch confirmed warmly.

“It’s false, false! It’s either an attempt to slander me, or the hallucination of a madman,” Mitya still shouted. “He’s simply raving, from loss of blood, from the wound. He must have imagined it when he came to.... He’s raving.”
“Yes, but he noticed the open door, not when he came to after his injuries, but before that, as soon as he went into the garden from the lodge.”
“But it’s false, it’s false! It can’t be! He’s slandering me out of spite.... He couldn’t have seen it ... I didn’t come from the door,” Mitya gasped.
The prosecutor turned to Nikolay Parfenovitch and said to him impressively:
“Confront him with it.”
“Do you recognize this object?”
Nikolay Parfenovitch laid on the table a large, thick official envelope, on which three seals still remained intact. The envelope was empty, and slit open at one end. Mitya stared at it wide-eyed.

“It ... it must be that envelope of my father’s, the envelope that contained the three thousand roubles ... and if there’s inscribed on it — allow me — ‘For my little chicken’ ... yes — three thousand!” he shouted. “Do you see, three thousand, do you see?”
“Of course, we see. But we didn’t find the money in it. It was empty, and lying on the floor by the bed, behind the screen.”
For several seconds Mitya stood as though thunderstruck.

“Gentlemen, it’s Smerdyakov!” he suddenly shouted at the top of his voice. “It’s he who murdered him! He robbed him! No one else knew where the old man hid the envelope. It’s Smerdyakov, that’s clear now!”
“But you, too, knew about the envelope, and that it was under the pillow.”

“I never knew it. I’ve never seen it. This is the first time I’ve looked at it. I only heard of it from Smerdyakov.... He was the only one who knew where the old man kept it hidden — I didn’t know ...” Mitya was completely breathless.
“But you told us yourself that the envelope was under your late father’s pillow. You specifically said it was under the pillow, so you must have known it.”
“We’ve got it written down,” confirmed Nikolay Parfenovitch.

“Nonsense! It’s absurd! I’d no idea it was under the pillow. And maybe it wasn’t under the pillow at all.... It was just a lucky guess that it was under the pillow. What does Smerdyakov say? Have you asked him where it was? What does Smerdyakov say? that’s the main point.... And I went out of my way to tell lies on myself.... I told you without thinking that it was under the pillow, and now you — Oh, you know how one says the wrong thing without meaning to. No one knew but Smerdyakov, only Smerdyakov, and no one else.... He didn’t even tell me where it was! But it’s his doing, his doing; there’s no doubt about it, he murdered him, that’s as clear as daylight now,” Mitya exclaimed, more and more frantic, repeating himself incoherently, growing more and more exasperated and excited. “You must understand that, and arrest him at once.... He must have killed him while I was running away and while Grigory was unconscious, that’s clear now.... He gave the signal and father opened to him ... because no one but he knew the signal, and without the signal father would never have opened the door....”

“But you are again forgetting the fact,” the prosecutor observed, still with the same restraint, though with a note of triumph, “that there was no need to give the signal if the door already stood open when you were there, while you were in the garden....”
“The door, the door,” muttered Mitya, and he stared speechless at the prosecutor. He sank back helpless in his chair. All were silent.
“Yes, the door!... It’s a nightmare! God is against me!” he exclaimed, staring before him in complete stupefaction.

“There, you see,” the prosecutor went on with dignity, “you can judge for yourself, Dmitri Fyodorovitch. On the one hand, we have the evidence of the open door from which you ran out — a fact that overwhelms both you and us. On the other hand, your incomprehensible, persistent, and, so to speak, obdurate silence about the source from which you obtained the money that was so suddenly seen in your hands, when only three hours earlier, by your own admission, you pledged your pistols for ten roubles! In the face of all these facts, judge for yourself. What are we to believe, and what can we rely on? And don’t accuse us of being ‘frigid, cynical, scoffing people,’ incapable of believing in the generous impulses of your heart.... Try to put yourself in our position ...”
Mitya was indescribably agitated. He turned pale.
“Very well!” he exclaimed suddenly. “I will tell you my secret. I’ll tell you where I got the money!... I’ll reveal my shame, so that I won’t have to blame myself or you afterwards.”

“And believe me, Dmitri Fyodorovitch,” put in Nikolay Parfenovitch, in a voice of almost pathetic delight, “that every sincere and complete confession on your part at this moment may, later on, have an immense influence in your favor, and may, indeed, moreover —”
But the prosecutor gave him a slight shove under the table, and he checked himself in time. Mitya, in fact, had not heard him.
